questions.stem: A star like our Sun will eventually become a white dwarf. What is the correct sequence of stages for a Sun-sized star?

options.text: Nebula -> Main sequence -> Red giant -> Supernova -> White dwarf
Nebula -> Protostar -> Main sequence -> Red giant -> Planetary nebula -> White dwarf
Nebula -> Main sequence -> Red supergiant -> Supernova -> Neutron star
Nebula -> Protostar -> Main sequence -> White dwarf -> Red giant

questions.explanation: A Sun-sized star follows: nebula (cloud of gas and dust) -> protostar (gravitational collapse begins) -> main sequence star (stable hydrogen fusion) -> red giant (hydrogen runs out, outer layers expand) -> planetary nebula (outer layers ejected) -> white dwarf (hot, dense remnant core). Option A includes a supernova, which only happens to massive stars. Option C describes a massive star's life cycle. Option D has the stages in the wrong order.

questions.stem: During the main sequence stage, a star is stable. What two forces are balanced to maintain this stability?

options.text: Magnetic force pushing outward and electric force pulling inward
Radiation pressure (from fusion) pushing outward and gravitational force pulling inward
Centrifugal force pushing outward and friction pulling inward
Nuclear force pushing outward and electromagnetic force pulling inward

questions.explanation: A main sequence star is in hydrostatic equilibrium: the outward radiation pressure (produced by nuclear fusion reactions in the core) exactly balances the inward gravitational force (due to the star's enormous mass). If fusion stopped, gravity would cause the star to collapse. If gravity weakened, radiation pressure would cause the star to expand. This balance can last billions of years for Sun-like stars.

questions.stem: The elements heavier than iron found on Earth (such as gold, silver, and uranium) were formed by:

options.text: Nuclear fusion inside our Sun
Chemical reactions in Earth's core
Supernova explosions of massive stars that existed before our Solar System formed
Radioactive decay of lighter elements on Earth

questions.explanation: Elements heavier than iron require more energy to form by fusion than they release. They can only be created in the extreme conditions of supernova explosions, where there is enough energy to force nuclei together. These elements were scattered into space by supernovae that occurred before our Solar System formed, and were incorporated into the nebula from which the Sun and planets condensed. Our Sun (A) only fuses hydrogen into helium. Chemical reactions (B) do not create new elements.

questions.stem: A star with a mass much greater than the Sun reaches the end of its life. What is the most likely final remnant?

options.text: A white dwarf
A planetary nebula
A neutron star or black hole
A red giant

questions.explanation: Very massive stars end their lives in a supernova explosion. If the remaining core is between about 1.4 and 3 solar masses, it forms a neutron star. If the core exceeds about 3 solar masses, gravity is so strong that nothing can prevent collapse, forming a black hole. White dwarfs (A) are the remnants of lower-mass stars. A planetary nebula (B) is the ejected outer layers, not the final remnant. A red giant (D) is a stage before the final explosion, not the end state.

questions.stem: A protostar forms when a region of a nebula begins to collapse. What provides the energy that heats the protostar before nuclear fusion begins?

options.text: Chemical reactions between hydrogen and oxygen
Radioactive decay of elements in the nebula
Gravitational potential energy being converted to thermal energy as the gas compresses
Energy from nearby stars shining on the protostar

questions.explanation: As the gas cloud collapses under gravity, gravitational potential energy is converted to kinetic energy of the infalling particles, which then converts to thermal (heat) energy through collisions. This heats the protostar until it eventually becomes hot enough (about 15 million degrees) for hydrogen fusion to begin. Chemical reactions (A) do not produce enough energy. While radioactive decay (B) exists, it is insignificant compared to gravitational energy. External starlight (D) does not heat the core.
